newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine alliance shares blame for clashes--Menem.
newsitem.headline: Argentine alliance shares blame for clashes--Menem.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem on Friday said street fighting that broke out during Thursday's general strike was the work of "savages" and blamed the political opposition for much of the violence.
"We don't want any more savages or subversives on the streets of our nation, because yesterday we saw real cowards covering up their faces," Menem said in a speech in the northern province of Chaco.

On Thursday, the CTA and MTA unions proved they could stage at least a partially successful general strike, despite opposition from the country's main labor confederation, the CGT, which is loyal to the governing Peronist Party.

Protest roadblocks sprang up throughout the country, and most them were went off peacefully. But several became the focus for violence. Police fired rubber bullets and arrested scores of protestors, as small groups of youths in Balaclavas threw stones or lit pools of gasoline on the road.

The country's main opposition group, an alliance formed just weeks ago between the centrist Radical Party and the center-left Frepaso coalition, voiced wary support for the sentiment behind the strike but distanced itself from the form of protest chosen.
Still, Menem, referring to the Radicals' term in government from 1983-89, attacked the party.
"What short memories the people who governed until 1989 have," said Menem, "They criticize us, but many of them are responsible for yesterday's acts of violence."
He said the protestors who turned violent were "small groups, but they were intellectually backed by those who preach peace. They have clearly shown that they are against peace and democracy."
Frepaso leader Carlos Alvarez accused the government of trying to use the violence to alarm voters before October's midterm congressional elections.
"There are (violent) groups which are very useful and are just what the government needs for its purposes," Alvarez said, quoted by the private DyN news agency.
He said that small, ultra-leftist groups had infiltrated strike protests looking for trouble.

The opposition alliance, ahead in opinion polls for key seats in the October elections, wants to project a moderate image. It has vowed to keep key components of the Peronist government's economic program, which has slashed once rampant inflation to almost nothing but sent unemployment up to 16.1 percent.
